children: co-founder Michael Saylor are offering competing visions of how artificial intelligence will reshape the economy, with Musk predicting money could become largely unnecessary and Saylor arguing scarcity will always carry value.

In an interview with China Media Group released last week, Musk said he expects what he called "effectively universal high income," describing an age of abundance in which humanoid robots produce far more goods and services than people could use.

He repeated the idea Tuesday at the White House, telling reporters that superintelligence and robots would likely produce not just a universal basic income but a universal high income, with better medical care included. Musk made similar remarks in a July interview with The Economist, predicting money would stop mattering by 2036.

Saylor pushed back on the idea a month later, during an appearance on the Diary of a CEO podcast. Asked by host Steven Bartlett whether he agreed with Musk's prediction, Saylor argued that not everyone gets a Hamptons house, a private jet or a yacht, however abundant basic goods become.

He acknowledged AI could make essentials like housing and transportation far cheaper, even free, but contended that would shift spending toward rarer goods that signal status rather than eliminate money's role. People are status-oriented animals who will always want something more, he said, whether that means a bigger house or a car nicer than a neighbor's.
Saylor's argument doubles as the core case for Bitcoin

, which caps its total supply at 21 million coins. His company sold 3,588 bitcoin in July to fund investor payments but returned to buying in September, and now holds 847,666 bitcoin worth roughly $71 billion at recent prices.

Musk's timeline has drawn skepticism elsewhere too. Venture capitalist Vinod Khosla wrote that money would only stop mattering by 2036 if governments actually permit that level of abundance to reach people.

title: Michael Saylor Rejects Musk's Vision of a Moneyless Future
